summary: NASA Astronaut Physiology Portal (NAPP) is a server-hosted web application that integrates a health monitoring system across any spaceflight scenario, taking into account diverse environmental contexts and considering multiple vital parameters to be measured and registered. Our system is specially designed to aid astronauts, detect current health issues and prepare them to face future changes, while informing about the possible health problems and how to act about them. In case of an emergency, the app properly alerts not just user themselves but the whole mission crew.
details:
NAPP: A Mission-Aware Web Platform for Integrated Crew Health Monitoring in Human Spaceflight

Index Terms — human spaceflight, crew health monitoring, web application, real-time systems, clinical decision support, human-centred design.

1. Introduction

NAPP is a hosted web application for monitoring astronaut health during long-duration missions. A crew member selects a profile, enters a mission scene, and sees five vital signs — respiratory rate, heart rate, oxygen saturation, blood pressure, and skin temperature — together with five monitoring modules: cardiovascular health, cognition, sleep, radiation, and daily habits.

The platform reads historical telemetry from canonical CSV files, adds near-real-time samples from a live simulation, and propagates critical alerts only to the other members of the same mission. Its purpose is integration: one interface where a crew member can check current status, review trends, and see what changed, without opening separate devices, files, or paper checklists.

The current version is a research prototype built on simulated data. It is not a diagnostic device.

2. How It Works – Our Technical Insight

Two-layer architecture. The client and the server have separate responsibilities. The Angular client owns presentation, interaction, and local preferences; the Node server owns identity, mission membership, canonical telemetry, and fan-out. Because of this split, a module can render before historical data arrive, and the server never performs clinical interpretation.

CSV as the shared source of truth. Each domain has one file: 28 days of cardiovascular samples at five-minute intervals with blood pressure every 30 minutes, one row per night for sleep, hourly radiation measurements, and daily habit records. CSV was chosen over a database for telemetry because it is inspectable, portable, and easy to regenerate. At start-up the backend checks whether the cardiovascular file is missing, future-dated, or older than ten minutes; if so, it regenerates it with a deterministic Python generator that accepts an end time and a seed.

Throttled write-back instead of streaming. Real-time behaviour is deliberately modest. The cardiovascular page creates a sample every 1.5 seconds, updates blood pressure every twenty beats, but persists to the server at most every five minutes. This avoids two failure modes: a UI that depends on a continuous connection, and a canonical file that grows without bound during a demonstration.
